utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue hearing any evidence, the Chamber establishes that Mr. Markac is not present and that Mr. Gotovina is not present. The Chamber was informed that the reasons for Mr. Markac and Mr. Gotovina not being present in court today is that they wanted to protest against events that happened yesterday in Croatia. Whatever the Chamber knows about it is hearsay, but in a motion which was filed this morning by the Gotovina Defence, it was - and I'm summarising - it was stated that yesterday arrests took place. Among the persons arrested in Croatia were members of the Gotovina Defence team, and that search and seizure -- search of premises occupied by members of the Defence team of Mr. Gotovina, and that a search of the Gotovina Defence - could I say "centre" - at least the premises where the Defence is prepared, that there were searches and there were seizures, including computers. That is the information, again briefly, which is contained in the motion which was filed this morning. I'll come to that motion in a minute. The first matter to be considered is whether or not to proceed in the absence of two of the accused, and let us first hear from the parties, whether there are objections against proceeding in the absence of these two accused. You can want to make a protest at the same time, that not necessarily implies that you have instructed counsel not to proceed. If we can't proceed -- that might also include that we can't proceed on the matters raised in the motion. I mean, there's not such a thing as 75 per cent of the trial. Mr. Misetic, could I hear whether you received instructions to object against proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, our instructions are to object to proceeding with the testimony of witnesses. However, my client has instructed us to fully address the procedural issues involved and the events that took place yesterday and that, as we speak, are continuing to taking place. And I can provide additional information to the Chamber on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps it's good to -- at a later stage to hear -- The Chamber will consider whether it accepts the conditions, if I could call them like that -- of course, Mr. Gotovina can instruct you as he wishes. But whether the Chamber feels that it's bound to say, Well, you may proceed, but only with those matters and not with other matters, how that should be considered in light of the use of the right of an accused to attend at his trial. We'll consider that, I would say, in a moment, after we have dealt with some procedural matters. Could I receive information from the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our instructions are similar. Obviously, we're in our Defence case, and we have not received permission from our client to continue with presentation of evidence without his presence. But similarly with General Gotovina's discharge to his counsel, we have been given the authority, at least as of today, to discuss this procedural issue, so that's where we stand as well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, the Chamber will consider whether such conditions or such limits on how we could proceed or not are to be understood, and the matter may be even more urgent for the Markac Defence because you are presenting your evidence at this moment. But I'm not anticipating anything. I'm just observing that your situation may be even a bit different from the Gotovina Defence. At this moment, therefore, we do not consider that we proceed at this moment, against the wishes of either the Markac Defence or the Gotovina Defence. Again, what decision is to be taken at a later stage is another matter. Now, let me just -- yes. I am just looking at ... Mr. Misetic, the Chamber was copied on a form, "Absence from court," it says, "due to illness," but that's only the title of that form. The first box which is to be ticked if you're unable to attend court proceedings on this date due to illness, is not ticked. The second box, which contains the text: "I have discussed the matter with my counsel," is ticked by Mr. Gotovina. The third box reads: "I understand that I have a right to be present at all trial proceedings against me. However, I waive my right to be present in court on this date and give my consent for the proceedings to continue in my absence, but in the presence of my counsel." That box has been ticked. And from what I see, it appears in also the language of Mr. Gotovina. I just put all this on the record so that I know that there's no confusion about that. Then we also have received an "Absent from court due to illness" form apparently in relation to Mr. Markac, which is not -- none of the boxes has been ticked. We have a second page wherein the principal officer states that he confirms receipt of this form from the detainee named over at 1335, and that the detainee refuses to sign. And as other comments from the principal officer, Mr. Markac believes his human rights have been violated. He doesn't want his lawyer to continue with the hearings in his absence. This is Mr. Markac's decision, not the lawyer's. And then at the bottom, it says: "Non-medical." Apparently there's no illness at stake. That is what the Chamber has received. And as far as Mr. Gotovina is concerned, apart from how we have to interpret the form, Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Markac says that he doesn't want his lawyers to continue, and there's no reservation whatsoever -- it says "with the hearings in his absence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, earlier today, as soon as I learnt about the events, I visited Mr. Markac in the Detention Unit. I explained the situation to him. And after that, he made the decision the way he did. I don't believe that the interpretation that the official has provided and put on paper is correct, in light of the instructions of my client, who said that he authorised us Defence counsel to attend the procedural discussion about the problem, but he also instructed us not to proceed with further presentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whatever position the Chamber will take in this respect. Now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me. With regard to the form filled out by our client - we're putting this on the record - General Gotovina, on the second page, stated that: "Mr. Gotovina told me, the writer, that his lawyer will explain the matter in court." Just for the sake of fullness of the record, and completeness, I just put that on the record, because that is in the same space that General Markac's comments have been noted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just checking whether I overlooked the second page or whether I did not receive it. I hope, Mr. Kehoe, that you will understand that this information comes to us at this moment by e-mail and, therefore, has not got the thorough attention as we usually give to written submissions or written documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my comments were not one of criticism, but just one of completeness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I missed the second page, as a matter of fact. And for the completeness of the record, it reads: "Mr. Gotovina told me that his lawyer will explain the matter in court." And it also states that it apparently is not a medical issue. Thank you for completing the record in this respect. Now, any observations as far as the Prosecution is concerned to proceed under the present circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. We had absences from the accused in the past, and they were represented by counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We want to proceed. Whether we should also proceed with hearing the evidence is to be considered if we are at a point where we would restart hearing the evidence. So, therefore, at this moment it seems there are no objections against proceeding at least on the matters as -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That there are objections from the Defence, yes. But we are ready to proceed, and I think we should proceed with the presentation of evidence. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that point perhaps soon. Mr. Misetic, let me just check again. I started saying what the information was the Chamber had received. Now, we have certainly received most of the information in the motion that was filed today, which gives an update on the investigatorial and prosecutorial activity of the Croatian authorities in relation to, among others, as I understand -- against members of the Gotovina Defence team. I think I said that they were arrested. This may be due to the fact the Chamber staff has informed the Judges about telephone conversations which have taken place yesterday evening, in which information on the events was contained as well. That was rather summary. When I said that members had been arrested, it may well be that -- because that's not to be found in the motion, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would have to check the motion, Mr. President. I can tell you that -- and I'm not an expert in Croatian law or Croatian legal terminology, but Mr. Ivanovic has been arrested. Two investigators, I guess the word would be, were "detained ," but all three had official Gotovina Defence documents and/or computers seized, and they are all now in the possession of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you use the word "detained," that is that you wanted to express that matters happened yesterday which did not allow them to freely move where they wanted to go at all times; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That and -- Mr. Mikulicic would know better than I, but I understand the distinction also under Croatian law triggers whether there is a right to counsel to be present or not, so the detainees did not have a right to counsel. Mr. Ivanovic, as an arrested person, did have his counsel present, but only after he arrived in Zagreb, after having been detained by the police on the highway travelling to Split and forcibly brought back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what the Chamber would -- let's try to clearly separate two matters. The first is what the Defence is seeking in the motion; that is, the presence of Mr. Brammertz with all relevant material with him at the meeting of next Wednesday - I think it was Wednesday - with the Croatian government, the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to confess that because events are fluid, were fluid, and continue to develop, we were going to today appear in court and, pursuant to Rule 73, make additional oral motions in terms of the relief we seek. That was the status yesterday. We obviously had all night and this morning to consider further, consult with, I think, general counsels from various law firms that are involved in this case. Mr. Kehoe will address the Chamber on the specifics of the legal remedies we seek and what we think the legal issues are here. I can just state at this point that, first, it's not simply an issue of the accused having issues with what transpired yesterday. We need to alert the Chamber that we, as Defence counsel, cannot proceed in a situation where, for example, General Gotovina's communications with me in court are passed on by me to Mr. Ivanovic, and all of that is now in the possession of the Croatian government, presumably can be and might be turned over to the Prosecution. We have no idea what's in the hard drives of the computers that were seized, and we have no assurance at this point at this Tribunal that anything we say, anything we communicate from the courtroom is not going to be protected under the attorney-client privilege and a work-product document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's I think -- yes, it's clear to the Chamber that the present situation, which means members of the Gotovina Defence team not free to move as they wish, is that still the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, as I just received the chat, is still under arrest and is still in a police station, and has been detained since approximately 1.00 p.m. -- I should say has been arrested since approximately 1.00 p.m. yesterday. I do feel the need, Your Honour, to correct the record, in terms of the facts that you laid out, just so that there's no confusion. The Gotovina Defence has two offices in Zagreb. One of those offices was seized yesterday, and seized in the sense that police were present and sealed the office, waiting for Mr. Ivanovic to be brought back forcibly from Split, because as I understand under Croatian law, an attorney -- when an attorney office is searched, there are certain procedures and he needs to be present. There is a second office which has not yet been searched, although obviously we do not know what additional measures the Croatian government may take. But as I understand it, the search of the law office -- the first law office was completed sometime around 1.00 p.m. today. So in addition to the three computers seized yesterday, I am not certain whether additional computers were seized, but I did want to correct the factual record on that point. In terms of the relief we seek, I would, with your leave, Mr. President, ask Mr. Kehoe to address that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first try to see whether there's an update as far as the facts are concerned. Mr. Ivanovic is still not free to move as he wishes. Any other members of the Gotovina Defence team which are in a similar situation, as far as you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As of this morning, no, Mr. President, but they were detained and released yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And these were which members of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One is a -- one is Jozo Ribicic, who the Chamber will see his name on a few of the statements that the Defence put in evidence. The other is a former member of the Gotovina Defence, Mr. Zeljko Hucic. But, nevertheless, I don't know what information was seized from him, so -- he did not have a computer seized. Mr. Ribicic and Mr. Ivanovic did have computers seized, and they continue to be members of the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, not to say that that is critical, but since the matter has been raised in relation to Mr. Ivanovic before, was Mr. Ribicic accredited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Not accredited to appear in the courtroom, but disclosed to the Registrar on the list of members of the Gotovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's like the first step, as with Mr. Ivanovic, whereas at a later stage, as the Chamber understands from the Registry, primarily for having access to certain systems, that then a formal accreditation letter was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's that, but there's also a very critical thing for the Chamber, which is by disclosing these individuals to the Registrar, pursuant to the Chamber's order of the 14th of July, 2006, that is how we control and guarantee the Chamber the security of witness information, protective measures, et cetera, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no question about that. But just to say that it has been argued, whether that argument is valid or not, that the accreditation, only the second one, would be valid and not the first one, I'm not pronouncing anything. I'm just finding out whether Mr. Ribicic -- what formalities were fulfilled. And I do understand that he was reported to the Registry as a member of the -- he was identified and reported to the Registry as a member of the Gotovina Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, as was Mr. Hucic, who was then subsequently -- as we make changes in the team, we are to update the list, and his name was subsequently removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since when is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it is since -- I'll have to check, but I believe it's since April of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ribicic was identified as a member when?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be the first filing, so July of 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, apart from what to do with the information, but is there any other update as far as the facts are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not positive anymore how much I've said and how much is in the motion, but I don't believe so, Your Honour. And you'll forgive me if I've forgotten something, I will alert you, but that is essentially the status of affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there's nothing on this on your mind at this moment. You say, Well, this factual update should be known to the Chamber at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Chamber is aware that there are various aspects involved in the present situation. But before I elaborate on that, is there any factual information the Prosecution would like to add to what the Chamber knows until now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then early -- yes, Mr. Mikulicic, any further factual information to be provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I have nothing further to add. I would like to say a couple of words in order to explain the Markac Defence position regarding this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that I first identify areas of which the Chamber, at this moment, found to be involved in the present situation, and then, of course, you will have an opportunity to further comment on certain matters. Earlier, the Chamber spent quite some time on the issue of immunity. The immunity issue is still prominently there at this moment. Although the Chamber usually does not give any insight in its working and its methods, a meeting was scheduled for tomorrow to finalise the draft on the last motion for a restraining order to Croatia. That is an issue which was involved in the present situation and is still, as I said, prominently involved. However, the new facts add to that, that there may be legitimate concerns about the duties the Gotovina Defence has in relation to confidentiality -- both confidentiality to be observed as a result of orders of this Chamber, that is, confidential information about identity of witnesses, it's confidential information about documents which were admitted under seal. The whole lot of that is now also, I would say, in the core of the matter. A third matter which now becomes very important is also the disturbance in the confidentiality of the relation between counsel and client, professional privilege. That's a third area I would like to point out the Chamber is aware of, that it is affected or most likely be affected by the present situation. Of course, we do not know yet what has been done with the computers and with the information, but there is a great likelihood that that matter is being affected. The fourth element the Chamber discerns is practical operation of the Defence and the preparation of the Defence, what material is not available anymore, what communications are disturbed under the present circumstances. That is a fourth area the Chamber has identified as being affected by the present situation. Now, having identified these areas, having looked at what is alleged in the motion by the Gotovina Defence, the situation may be -- of course, a lot depends on the solidity of the factual basis of the allegations. The Chamber can't anticipate on that in any way. We've heard, until now, the position of the Gotovina Defence. But if these allegations - and I emphasise "if" - were true, the Chamber considers the situation of -- the situation as very serious. Let there be no doubt about that. That's also the reason why we pay immediate attention to this matter. The Chamber was alerted -- received a courtesy copy earlier, and immediately started thinking about what happened. Now, one remedy sought is in the motion. The Chamber will understand that there may be more remedies, but before we continue with other remedies, the Chamber would first like to briefly consider the remedy sought, which is Mr. Brammertz to appear on the hearing next week with Croatia and to bring all relevant material with him. That is the remedy sought to the subpoena duces tecum. My first question, Mr. Kehoe, to you: Any other remedies you would seek, would they make moot the first remedy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They would not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, under those circumstances, I would like to briefly pay attention to the first remedy sought. Mr. Waespi, could you inform the Chamber whether Mr. Brammertz either spontaneously - I think his position allows him to do so - or if being invited by the Chamber, or if being strongly requested by the Chamber, would appear and bring the documents -- what to do with them is a second matter, but at least to bring them, that's the first question, because if we're talking about a subpoena, a subpoena is usually issued if a person is not voluntarily doing what he is expected to do. Now, I earlier had on my list to -- that first to inquire with you whether Mr. Brammertz can be reached. Well, since I happened to see him in the corridor 20 minutes ago, he cannot be far away. Can you answer that question already, or would you first have to consult with Mr. Brammertz?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know about the availability of the Prosecutor, but as you know, we received a courtesy copy of the motion last night. It's been officially filed today. We are looking to it, and we'll reply in writing by the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not an answer to my question. And the proceedings -- my question is -- let me be clear. Of course, the Chamber will decide on the motion. The Chamber will have to decide, and then, of course, we'll have to hear the response by the Prosecution. However, if Mr. Brammertz would appear, then, of course, that remedy would be moot. And I can imagine, in view of the allegations raised, that there is a certain interest in -- even without even being invited, but certainly when invited or even strongly requested, to come, which would make the first -- but if you say -- I would invite you to inquire that with Mr. Brammertz and give an answer to that question. And if the answer is, Under no circumstances I will appear here, but only if ordered, subpoenaed, call it whatever you want to call it, by the Chamber, then it's clear that the Chamber will have to decide the matter, and of course we would decide that matter after we have heard the response by, in this case, the Prosecution. The question is for Mr. Brammertz. The response is expected from the Prosecution. In this case, I'm not going into any details at this moment about the internal hierarchy, but I would address you to hear about the response, and I also address you to inquire with Mr. Brammertz whether he would not come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that, if possible by the end of tomorrow in a filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Waespi, I'm asking you to inquire with Mr. Brammertz. And if he wants to think about it for a day, that's fine. That means that he does not express himself in the way I mentioned; that is, that he has not made up his mind as to whether or not to appear, if either spontaneously, or if being invited, or if being strongly requested to do so. So we would like to have an answer to that. If he has not made up his mind, the answer is that we do not know, and then we have to proceed with the -- and then, of course, the Chamber will -- under those circumstances, will set the time-limit for a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- because you ask me, I have talked to him yesterday, after we have received the filing, and the result was we will file our response by the end of Friday. If you want a response earlier, I don't know what his disposition -- his state of mind is today. If you want an earlier response, I can get back to him. But we have, as of yesterday, not made up our mind, except for the fact that we would in respond in writing, if invited to do so, by the end of tomorrow. That's the current state of mind I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to seek this point of view to be reconfirmed, because you say it's the current state of mind you have. If that is the current state of mind of Mr. Brammertz, we'd like to know that as quickly as possible so that we can further consider how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted -- before we stray a little further, I wanted to add, the Chamber mentioned on page 13, line 3: "The third matter which now becomes very important is also the disturbance in the confidentiality of the relation between counsel and client, professional privilege." If the Gotovina computers, and we assume that they do, contained information over which there is a joint Defence privilege, then that privilege has been compromised as to our client as well. So we are a part of that third prong that the Court has identified. And we do have share, obviously, information, we have joint issues that we deal with in the Defence, so that issue with respect to the compromisability of information related to our client is also very, very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that point. Of course, we will have to consider that. At the same time, it seems to be a very interesting issue that if you share it with others who also have a privilege, to what extent it has been shared with outsiders or not, but that is a matter, I take it, for this moment that you put on the record, that the violation counsel-client privilege may have a further effect on -- not just limited to the Gotovina Defence, but could include the other Defence teams as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And for those reasons and for those potential issues, I've had to notify my law firm's general counsel of this situation. So we will also be weighing in through our general counsel on that, because it affects -- directly affects our lawyer-client relationship and the privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone is busy, that's for sure. I'd now like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier said that I would deal with the first remedy sought and then with the others. Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber invites you to make any further submissions, even if that would result in oral motions. Two matters I would like to bring to your attention. The first is that where I pointed at the four areas the Chamber considers to be of a kind to experience an impact of the present situation, of course, I've not explained all the things that are on the mind of the Chamber, so, therefore, pointing at them is to indicate that there may be -- again depending on the factual basis of it, that there may be a serious situation, and of course we are thinking about more than just identifying privilege or that. I mean, the Chamber, as a professional bench, is, of course, aware of the major issues involved in privilege, in obligations to keep confidential, what the limits are; that if beyond your will you lose control of certain material, that you're not mastering the situation. I mean, just to tell you that the Chamber has more on its mind, and that we'd first like to have a brief introduction on reasons and remedies sought. The second is that the Chamber, after having heard your submissions, will consider whether or not we would continue by hearing the submissions orally or whether the Chamber would be in need of further written submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We reserve our position in relation to that, and you're invited to proceed. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we briefly turn into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kehoe, I invited you to make any further submissions. And since I will further consult with VWS, I take it that whatever the outcome should be, that you will take that into account if --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just before I begin, I was given a note by my colleague Mr. Misetic to update the Chamber on the facts. Mr. Ivanovic has now been released and is in our Zagreb office. Should the Chamber have any additional inquiries the Chamber would like to pass on to him, we would be glad to do so, because he is sitting in our offices in Zagreb now, as I said. The other remedies that we would request orally, Mr. President, and I understand that the Chamber has asked Mr. Brammertz or invited Mr. Brammertz to attend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have not done yet, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But contemplating that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would ask the Chamber to likewise think about asking Mr. Bajic to make an appearance on Wednesday, as we requested in paragraph 8 of our subpoena. With regard to remedies that we request specifically right now, we ask for a cease and desist order, or, at the minimum, a temporary restraining order, for several things, and we ask for this pursuant to Rule 73: At this juncture, to seize all actions against Mr. Ivanovic at this juncture; and stop all searches of records and computers that the Republic of Croatia has in their possession; and to stop any contemplated -- or cease and desist from any contemplated searches they may think about doing against Gotovina Defence offices and/or personnel. Those are the immediate issues that I believe are necessary, Mr. President, in order for us to assess where we are vis-a-vis any potential breaches of the attorney-client privilege. And we ask for that cease and desist order to stay in place until the Chamber has made a final decision on these matters. So for lack of a better term, and to be somewhat pedestrian, we ask for the Chamber to just freeze in place everything that is going on right now and order the Republic of Croatia to take no further steps until further orders from this Court have been issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't mean to interrupt my colleague. Along those lines, we didn't obviously file the motion; we joined in support of the motion. But we also would like any preventive measure -- or we would like a preventative measure of the prohibition of this happening to us, including our offices in Zagreb and members of our team as well, one of whom is potentially -- or has been discussed by the Office of the Prosecutor and by the Croatian officials as well. And I'm not going to get into the details of that. But the potential exists for the same thing to happen to us, and that's something we obviously would want to avoid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Kuzmanovic was concerned whether he interrupted you, but I got the impression that you had raised what additional remedies on the same grounds, as I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the factual grounds to be completed by the information which was provided today to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then check exactly on whether -- yes. Let's take it step by step. The presence of Mr. Bajic, you said, as you had requested -- well, of course, it was not part of the remedy you sought in the motion, but you suggested that it might be good to have Mr. Bajic present. We have no idea yet on whether Mr. Bajic would come voluntarily or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to the Chamber that although not having yet received the answer of the Prosecution, but as matters stand now and not in the possession of their position, it seems to be reasonable to prepare for Mr. Bajic's presence. Now, any specific form? If the Chamber would invite the Government of Croatia to include Mr. Bajic in the delegation which will be present next week, would that do, or would you like to have anything else? I want to be clear on what remedies and in what form you're seeking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Bajic, Mr. President, be it by invitation or by a subpoena, we would again ask for akin to a subpoena duces tecum, for him to bring with him any and all instructions and memorandum received from the Office of the Prosecutor, similar to the information as detailed regarding the documents we requested from Mr. Brammertz. So, essentially, we would like from Mr. Bajic that which he received from Mr. Brammertz concerning this continuing investigation into a multitude of individuals and people, not the least of which is the individuals that we discussed today. We would like Mr. Bajic, as with Mr. Brammertz, to appear before the Chamber and that the parties have an opportunity to question Mr. Bajic and Mr. Brammertz, and for the Chamber to do as well. So it would be a subpoena duces tecum, or if it's an invitation, an invitation to bring with him the documents that he has on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's be very practical. An invitation is sent rather quickly, if we decide to do so. A subpoena is, of course, a bit of a different matter because that has to be drafted. Usually, if a request for a subpoena is there, unlike a request for an invitation, that a decision is taken on that, that we have to go through all the requirements usually applicable for issuing a subpoena. It would then have to be translated, it would have to be formally served first on the Government of Croatia and then served upon the person involved. I suggest to you that the Chamber, without delay, further inquires in a similar way as I did with Mr. Brammertz, inquire whether Mr. Bajic would appear if invited to do so. And perhaps to add to that, that the Government of Croatia is invited to make him a member of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do appreciate the practical concerns for issuing a subpoena, and that's why we didn't ask for a specific remedy and just put it on the table as something for the Chamber to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This, then, also means that we'll not start working immediately on the subpoena. It may well be that within a couple of hours we would know that we would not do without a subpoena. But under those circumstances, of course, we'd have to ask the Prosecution whether there would be any objection against such a motion to issue a subpoena. Mr. Waespi, you know the circumstances, as far as to say it inelegantly, to get Mr. Bajic into the courtroom, what would be the position if it would be necessary to make him appear in the courtroom unless being subpoenaed? Would you oppose against issuing such a subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As with the subpoena in relation to Mr. Brammertz, this is based, I think, on paragraph 1 or 2 on the factual speculation, I'll call it like that, on why a subpoena has to be issued on the facts. So having said that, Mr. Bajic appeared as a witness here. I don't think he was subpoenaed. So, you know, if he chose voluntarily to come - again, I'm not talking about the facts supporting a subpoena - I don't think we would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say even where you reject the allegations, that nevertheless you would not oppose against the issuance of a subpoena if need would be. Usually, we do not discuss subpoenas in public, but, Mr. Kehoe, that's, in the present situation, difficult to avoid because we can't lose pace at this moment. That is clear. Then, let's take it, as I said, step by step, and I started with page 21, lines 7 to 9. You asked for a cease and desist order or a temporary restraining order pursuant to Rule 73. You're seeking that it would be ordered to cease all actions against Mr. Ivanovic. That's one. Second, you seek an order that all searches of records and computers that the Republic of Croatia has in their possession. I understand this to be that you are seeking an order that the Republic of Croatia stops searching of the content of the computers and the content of the records which they have seized in the premises where the Gotovina Defence works --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As well as the individual computers taken from these individuals, as they have information contained thereon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, including the content of computers which were seized from members of the Gotovina team, even if not found in the premises, the offices in which the Gotovina Defence works. Let me see whether we have now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by some factual clarification, Mr. President, as to what I'm talking about on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would like to ... Yes. What you then next are seeking is a "cease and desist" order, to desist from any future searches against Gotovina Defence offices and/or personnel. This is a separate category. That's not stop searching what has already been seized, but to cease and desist from any future searches and seizures. And the temporal scope of such orders would at least be until the Chamber has made a final decision on these matters. And that would cover all of the remedies you are seeking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, you said you -- let me see. You would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just with regard to the computers, there was the office computers, and I do believe that Mr. Misetic referred to this. There was a computer that was in the possession of Mr. Ivanovic that had information, as well as Mr. Ribicic, as they were travelling. Those were two separate computers that were Gotovina Defence computes that were seized. Just by way of clarification, I was attempting to -- or maybe inartfully attempting to refer to those items; not just stuff in the office, but computers that the Republic of Croatia took from these gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I had understood. And when we're talking about Gotovina Defence members, we are talking about members present and former members, with the purpose of protecting any information which is still with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by one other point of clarity. When I was asking for a "cease and desist" order on all actions against Mr. Ivanovic, I was referring to, obviously, this most recent arrest, but also a request to cease and desist or suspend the proceedings that are currently underway at which Mr. Misetic was scheduled to go to tomorrow, or at least attend tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm concerned for Mr. Ivanovic, because as the Court is aware, I was supposed to testify tomorrow. In light of what transpired today, I felt compelled to appear before the Chamber on these matters. I don't know what is going to take place tomorrow, but, again, even with respect to those proceedings, we don't ask that they be, at this point, terminated, but if we could, as Mr. Kehoe said, just stop things from continuing to unfold until such time as both the Chamber and the parties here can establish factually what exactly has transpired in the last two days and what led up to what transpired. I think it would be very important, because absent that, then the potential injury could be such that by the time the Chamber issues a final ruling, the damage has already been done and information has already been reviewed and perhaps even internally disseminated within the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took the words "all actions against Mr. Ivanovic" to include all investigative and all prosecutorial action pending or contemplated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now looking at the parties, whether there's any other matter at this very moment to be raised, and then I'll confer with my colleagues how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter at this moment to be addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will need some time to consider the present situation. And I add again to that, that the situation, irrespective of whether the allegations have any ground, that the situation is considered to be a serious one, a very serious one. I add to that I would have one or two more questions for the Gotovina Defence of a rather technical nature. We would then suggest that we would adjourn for up to an hour or five-quarters of an hour, and then return into the courtroom. At the same time, I would invite the Gotovina and Markac Defence to see whether they can have any contact with their clients and to see whether their decision, because I understand that's what it was, and their instructions are still standing. I'm saying this because we have various interests at stake. We have, for example - and the Chamber can't ignore that - we have a witness waiting to complete his evidence. We have a general obligation to use court time as good as we can. It might well be that after this hour, the Chamber says, No further hearings because we need our time to do other things. All options are open. Nevertheless, I invite the Markac Defence and the Gotovina Defence to seek the present view, also in view, perhaps, of how the Chamber responded initially on the matter and the way in which we proceeded. I do not in any way anticipate, in this respect, on what the Chamber's decision would be if the accused would oppose against further proceeding, even if that would result in a remaining inactive by counsel. What the procedural consequences of such a situation would be is to be considered by the Chamber. And by inviting you to contact your clients, I do not in any way anticipate, either in one direction or in another direction, on what would follow. The very technical questions I would have are the following: Two times, we find a reference to Rules 70(B) and Rule 70(F) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That is what we usually call the Rule 70 information. Now, the Chamber wonders whether the Gotovina Defence offers to provide the Chamber with the names of potential witnesses, but subject to the protections of Rule 70(B) and Rule 70(F). Now, if I understand Rule 70(B) correctly, it says that information provided for further investigative purposes, and not to be used as evidence, should not be revealed. It's totally unclear to me why the Chamber, with these reservations, would receive names which I think, as a matter of fact, if it's real Rule 70(B), then I take it it's about the content of the statements, but then it -- it only mentions names, and then to say, Well, these names -- well, for evidence, for evidentiary purposes, they could not be used. I mean, what should the Chamber then possibly do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I said, upon reflection, perhaps we should have invoked a different Rule. But as I said last night, the situation was fluid. What we intended to indicate to the Chamber was that we could provide -- in terms of telling the Chamber what our good-faith basis is for making these allegations, we have individuals who have communicated this information to us. To be perfectly frank, without trying to be argumentative with the Prosecution, these individuals have concerns about potential ramifications to them, personally, and in the ongoing context of the assessments of Croatia's co-operation with Mr. Brammertz in his office that Mr. Brammertz might make about disclosing that information to Mr. Brammertz, about who passed that information along. What Rule and how we are to proceed obviously is a difficult situation, which I recognise, but I did not want the Chamber to think that we were making statements to the Chamber that we did not have a good-faith basis to believe. And we wanted to indicate generally who these persons were so that the Chamber had specific names, if it wished to obtain them, as to who it is that passed this information on to us. And that was the intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber may be hesitant - but I still have to discuss it with my colleagues - may be hesitant to receive names knowing in advance that it would be exclusively in the hands of the provider of the information on whether it could be used in evidence or not, because names, as such -- but perhaps you would --- those names might be related to positions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. And if -- I should say perhaps we should have also -- I believe I looked at Rule 69, which only references the Prosecution; however, I don't know whether it would also apply to the Defence, in terms of non-disclosure of the identity of a victim or witness who may be in danger or at risk, until such person is brought under the protection of the Tribunal. That is Rule 69(A). So -- and then obviously Rule 75. So I don't know what the issues would be, but these persons would be extremely reluctant to have their identities revealed in the political context that the parties find themselves in currently. Again, I just wish to reiterate, Mr. President, it's solely -- it was included by us because we understand that the allegations are serious, and we did not wish to fail to disclose to the Chamber the basis upon which the allegations were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will consider that matter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know you're going to take a break. Can we go into private session just for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll take a break. At this moment, we anticipate that we would resume at resume at 5.00, but this not a guarantee. But on from 5.00 the parties are requested to remained standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to apologise for the late start, but I sympathise with all those that have been waiting. We'll first move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The first matter I would like to deal with is the time-limit for a response. Mr. Waespi, the Chamber has considered the potential seriousness of the situation and the urgency of the situation, and orders the Prosecution to file its response by tomorrow noon. And this is a decision under Rule 136 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the Chamber has spent most of the time on the question how to proceed. We'd first like to have at least one piece of information. In the motion, Mr. Misetic, it is explained that the matter in which the arrests and the searches and seizures were taken are not unrelated to the -- well, let's say the 54 bis or the -- do you have any further information? Is there any description, as far as for the investigation of what offence committed, when, where? Is it still the same issue, or is it a follow-up issue? Could you give us any further factual information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will first do it in public session, and then we would need to move into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you. You know the answers. You know whether we need to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The public answer is that throughout the day yesterday, and including today, from what I can see on the internet, the Croatian government is saying that these actions are being done in close coordination with Mr. Brammertz. So to that extent, we're relying on public-source information concerning the reason that these activities are undertaken, and I simply do not see any reason to believe that the activities are unrelated to the Trial Chamber's 16 September 2008 order, and more specifically that these activities are in any way unrelated to Mr. Brammertz, because the Croatian government, including the prime minister yesterday, said publicly that she hopes, and I'm paraphrasing here, but she hopes Mr. Brammertz is going to be satisfied by what we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was primarily you could have said from the comments -- because I want to clearly separate two matters. The one is the action taken by; and the second question is: Who triggered it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I asked, as a matter of fact, details about the action taken yesterday, and the response was for 75 per cent about coordination -- well, let's say triggering matters. Do we have any clear information as this offence, committed on that day, consisting of burning documents, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. President, all I can say is people were -- except for Mr. Ivanovic, people were brought in, detained, the searches were conducted, and then released. So I can't say that there was a specific crime, other than the general standard crime which is always concealing and/or destroying archival documents, which is a legal classification for it. But there would be nothing in the warrants, as far as I know, that would then explain that this is at the instigation of the Office of the Prosecutor or the state prosecutor in Croatia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as far as the legal basis for searches and seizure are concerned, the most you can tell us, that it is under the same heading as the previous prosecutorial and investigative activities taken against Mr. Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Amongst others, though, yes. In other words, the same classification given to Mr. Ivanovic has now been expanded to include any number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we are still talking about the same qualification of the -- as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, as far as I'm aware. If we can -- I can then explain further, Your Honour, just what I understand to be happening in private session, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Waespi, I think we said that you would have to file your response, but I should first have asked whether your further consultation with Mr. Brammertz led to anything else than that he would insist on a written response rather than to express any willingness or unwillingness to appear in the session next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, during the break I did have a chance to consult with the Prosecutor, and wish to inform the Trial Chamber of the OTP position at this time as it regards the Defence motion, and also your remarks concerning the possibility of the Prosecutor appearing on this matter at this time. First, we consider that it is, at best, now premature to consider whether the Prosecutor should appear in any capacity in respect to this motion. The Trial Chamber has before it at this time only the assertions of Defence counsel, which are themselves based on unsubstantiated allegations of anonymous witnesses which form the basis of the motion. Before the Trial Chamber could begin to consider whether to invite the Prosecutor to appear on such a matter, the Defence would have to make a sufficient factual showing to justify the relief which it seeks. The Trial Chamber has no evidence before it at this time that would justify consideration of the question whether the presence of the Prosecutor is warranted. As regards the allegations contained in paragraphs 2 and 3 of the motion, the Prosecutor denies the allegations of misconduct in their entirety. In order to assist the Trial Chamber in resolving the matter as quickly and efficiently as possible, of course, the Prosecutor will file, by noon tomorrow, a detailed written response to these allegations. The Prosecutor's response will refer, for example, to information as reflected in the statement issued by the State Attorney's Office this afternoon, the state attorney of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if what you're saying is that we will receive a detailed written response in which we find -- I think at this moment the matter is so urgent that we'd rather not have a preview of what will be received on paper anyhow tomorrow by noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's fine. You were asking about new developments, and we thought it was important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say apart from what will be in there, I can add one thing. At the same time, I also stopped Mr. Misetic at a certain moment in time, because I said that we would not hear certain matters, that is, the link. We are mainly interested in whether it was a new issue or whether it was a continuation of an already assisting procedural context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is anything you would like to add in that respect, we would be glad to hear from you. If not, we will carefully read the submissions on our own. The Chamber has further considered whether it could issue the kind of orders sought, one subpoena to be issued, a subpoena duces tecum for Mr. Brammertz, but we meanwhile have a number of "cease and desist" orders as well. The Chamber, in the previous decisions in the Rule 54 bis matter, has stated that in exceptional circumstances it would consider that it would be competent to issue such order so as not to exclude once and forever that it could. That still is the position of the Chamber. At the same time, the Chamber thinks that it would be procedurally inappropriate to issue such heavy orders without even having heard responses both, in this case, from the Prosecution and from the Republic of Croatia. As I said before, the matter is not only potentially very serious, but also is very urgent. The Chamber has used part of the time available to explore the possibility to have a hearing tomorrow in the afternoon, at 2.00, after having received the response by the Prosecution, in which also the Republic of Croatia would appear. That hearing, if it will be scheduled -- and of course it takes quite some efforts to see whether this is possible, but the first actions are undertaken at this very moment. Of course, the first thing the Chamber would like to hear from the parties, whether they could be here. I mean, we had to check -- the Judges are there. Mr. Misetic, of course, the Chamber had on its mind also your intended trip to Zagreb, which we do not know exactly whether, under the present circumstances -- you may not have been perfectly clear on this matter, whether you had cancelled that or whether you would still be here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. President. It's impossible for me to be there by -- it was supposed scheduled for 8.15 tomorrow morning, and it's now impossible for me to be in Zagreb by then, so, yes, I've cancelled the trip, at some concern in light of what the consequences will be for that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, in some jurisdictions, if not in all, failing to appear as a witness is a matter which could be investigated, and the Chamber is fully aware of that. But at this moment, I'm focusing primarily on the practical side of a hearing tomorrow afternoon here in The Hague. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, because of the scheduling that we had, I have some other matter to take care of a personal nature. I do think, however, that Mr. Misetic can proceed in my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Misetic is lead counsel anyhow, so -- but you have introduced the motions. That's clear, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just correct the record, we're both lead counsel in the case, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't aware of that. I should have been, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the basis that there were no hearings tomorrow, I've made personal arrangements. I'm travelling to the United Kingdom tomorrow for personal reasons that I can't escape from, and unfortunately Mr. Kay and Ms. Higgins have gone home for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear your view on hearing this matter, which, of course, does not primarily focus on Mr. Cermak, in the absence of the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would need to speak to my client about that, and also to Mr. Kay, before basically waiving --- Mr. Cermak waiving his right to be present during that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cermak does not have to waive his right to be present. I mean, he can be present, even if that would -- of course, I can imagine that, as counsel, you would not be happy, Mr. Cermak to be present unrepresented and without your assistance, your guidance. But that is a matter to be explored for you, I would say, and it is one of the elements -- as I said before, we are exploring whether we can issue a scheduling order tomorrow morning, and the Chamber would like to hear from you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could take -- if the Court could take a break and so at least I can speak to Mr. Cermak about this, because this is an important personal matter, and otherwise, I'd cancel it, basically. And that's the problem I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone will be convinced that the Chamber is not seeking such hearings in order to find further amusement on Friday afternoon, which was supposed to be free. That is clear to everyone, I think. You want to consult right away with Mr. Cermak, or how much time do you think you'll need?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give you an opportunity, but not at this very moment, Mr. Cayley. But within a couple of minutes. Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will have no problem to attend tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No problem to attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The main purpose of the hearing tomorrow will be to hear views and submissions and positions in relation to a freezing order. That's what the Chamber will address first, not to say that the other orders as being sought would -- that we would not deal with them or that we would exclude to issue whatever order. But the main focus will be primarily on whether a situation in which everything is frozen can be achieved by whatever means. That is the main purpose. Of course, I can imagine that one says, Well, we'd rather have it already there tomorrow morning at 4.00, but we also have to be practical. The Chamber, as I said before, is not issuing orders before at least an opportunity has been given to the parties to respond or to be heard; not to say that if we couldn't hear the parties -- interested parties, that we would, under all circumstances, refrain from issuing orders, but at least this is a procedural requirement the Chamber takes seriously at this moment. From the fact that we deal with it tomorrow, it may be understood that the Chamber is fully aware of the urgency and the potential seriousness of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we will be focusing on the freezing of the situation, the Chamber would include in that any effect on the Markac Defence, because that was a matter of concern addressed. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interfere, but there's a practical problem we are facing, and this is the problem of a witness waiting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has informed the parties on everything it's wanted to inform the parties about. We have one hour left today. Anything to be raised which is of such urgency that it should be done immediately? Because I would then move to our next subject; that is, the witness waiting. Nothing. Then we have one hour left, and the Chamber was informed that the witness, also for urgent personal reasons, would have to return to Croatia. I do understand that a person had died, and that for that reason he has to return. Now, the cross-examination was scheduled for one to two sessions. First of all, whether we can continue at all depends on -- well, the Chamber would like to hear whether the Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence are still saying, We can't continue with hearing any evidence, even in the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break I spoke with my client, and his position remains the same. So we are not allowed to proceed with any evidence in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spoke with General Gotovina, who expresses his gratitude for the manner in which the Chamber addressed the issue. He supports General Markac's position, in that General Markac wishes to be present, and therefore would ask that Mr. Markac and he be allowed to be present for actual witness testimony. That's the message he wished to convey. On behalf of Mr. Kehoe and myself, we also wish to express our own personal concern about proceeding in a situation where we still essentially have the rights to the security of the attorney-client and work relationship and work product. And I understand the position that the Chamber is in and that we're dealing with this tomorrow, but there's still that uncertainty on our behalf, given that we don't know what access, including access the Croatian authorities may currently have to our communication capabilities at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be any different if you would hear some of the evidence to be given in cross-examination by the witness who's waiting and who wants to attend a funeral next week? That's my question to you. If that would significantly change, we would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can say is we sympathise with the witness and the position the Chamber is in. I also trust that the Chamber understands, from a legal perspective, the position that we're in. And so I guess we'll leave it in the Chamber's hands, then, how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the reasons for the absence of the two accused. The Chamber has considered the situation in which the witness finds himself at this moment. The Chamber has decided that we'll start the cross-examination of the witness, because that's what we're about to hear, and then to see -- to ask you, Mr. Waespi, to focus on core matters primarily and see what you could achieve in cross-examination in the next 55 minutes. I know that it's -- the Chamber will consider any further requests for recalling the witness, who has to leave. And meanwhile the Chamber offers to the accused that they'll be provided with a video of this afternoon's session, including the cross-examination of the witness. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Cayley, I do not know how urgent the cross-examination of this witness is for you. The Chamber would not mind if you would feel that it could be justified to leave the courtroom just briefly and consult with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for this witness, Your Honour, so I think that would be perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if it can be arranged that -- if it can be arranged that you meet with Mr. Cermak at this moment, then everyone who has to assist in that is invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vitez. The Chamber regrets that you had to wait for such a long time. The Chamber is informed about your personal circumstances and is seeking to achieve that we could finish your cross-examination. You would certainly help by giving short and focused answers. And I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Waespi will now cross-examine you. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Vitez. Let me go into the issue of Gracac with you. In your witness statement, at paragraph 4, you say that you arrived at about 1200 hours to the entrance of Gracac, and we know from your testimony yesterday that was in the Stikada area in Gracac. So that was on the 5th of August that you arrived with your units in Gracac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, where did your unit exactly go on the 5th of August? And perhaps we could have D433, a map. Did your unit go into Gracac, itself, or stay in Stikada all the time on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of that day on the 5th of August, my unit did not enter Gracac. We stayed in the territory of Stikada, and all that time we were by the Lake Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you look at the screen in front of you, you can see a map. Number 5 depicts Gracac; and number 7, the Stikada area. And we also see a lake there. Is that the lake?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, next to number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you continue in your witness statement that you said you stayed there until the following day: "On 6th August, we stayed in the area, resting and preparing for further activities." Now, did your unit stay together on the 6th of August by the lake?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that time, the entire unit -- the complete unit was by the lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you mentioned that you were in Loncari. We tried to find Loncari in this area, but couldn't find it. Can you tell us, on the map in front of you, where Loncari is. And perhaps with the help of the usher, you could mark "Loncari."

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was a hamlet just by the lake, on the lakeshores.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that would be near the location called Stikada.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's sufficient. Now, during your stay in Gracac, your policemen were pretty relaxed after you were entering Gracac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's get specific here. He said "Stikada," not "Gracac."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise. "Stikada" is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your unit -- your policemen were pretty relaxed when you were resting in Stikada; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one couldn't really say that they were relaxed. We could tend to the basic hygiene needs at the lake, and we were on standby all the time because we didn't know when and from where the enemy could turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you were swimming in the lake?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's no longer needed, Mr. Usher. I think we have a good idea where Loncari is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, we did have a swim, but it was not really long swimming for two hours. Individuals would enter the lake, stay a couple of minutes to have a wash, basically, more than anything else, and then got out and continued being in full combat gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's return to P1237. That's the report about the Varazdin -- the Varazdin unit activities we have looked at yesterday, which was authored by your commander. And it's English page 3 -- I apologise, English page 2. And in B/C/S, it's page 16, the actual page 16 numbered on top of the page, which is, I think, about the third page. And there, it's stated, in the middle of page 2, English: "We used the break to bathe in the nearby lake which we had been looking at from the tops of Mount Velebit for almost three years." That's an accurate description of what the policemen were doing and their state of mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already told you that each of us had 10 to 15 minutes to take a bath, and get out and continued doing whatever they were supposed to do; put on their combat gear, check their personal equipment, and be prepared, be at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I understand that on the 7th of August, your unit was ordered to leave the Stikada area again and proceed to Bruvno. Who ordered you to leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command or the order was received by my unit commander, and he had received it from our force's Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when, exactly, did you leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning hours, on the 7th, sometime in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now yesterday you told the Trial Chamber that on the 7th of August, when you were moving from Stikada towards Bruvno, and I quote you on page 25989: "What I can remember is damage. I saw several buildings that were destroyed, but as far as I remember they had been destroyed a long time previously. There had been vegetation growing out of the ruins. I don't remember any other damage." Now, were you aware that there were international observers in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for them being in Gracac, I don't know. I didn't see them. But we knew that there were a lot of international troops throughout the entire area where we were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you moved, on the 7th, from Stikada to Bruvno, did you go through Gracac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So where did you go in relation to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can look at D433. Perhaps that could be called back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So did you circumvent Gracac, then, or did you return back? Let me remind you number 5 is Gracac, number 7 is where you were, and obviously Bruvno would be to the north-east or upper left on this map. Can you tell me - and perhaps this time we would need Mr. Usher's assistance - the path you took? We can make it -- if you're happy with it, then it's fine. We could make it larger, if you want.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is okay. Thank you. We went to the right from Stikada. That's the route we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether you used actually the pencil. You need to touch the surface to make a marking.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been billeted here [marks], and then we took a bypass around Gracac and took this route towards Bruvno [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I think that's fine for the time being. If this could be tendered into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm addressing those Defence counsel who think they could express themselves on objections. Mr. Cayley, because you seem to be the only one who's instructed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that necessarily shows the way, because he says he wanted to bypass, and that looks like it's going right through the city. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then let's ask the witness. When you said, We took a bypass, on this map, as far as I can see, you drew a line which goes a bit south of the town, itself, and then east from town to go to the north again. Now, is that what you intended to depict on this map? Mr. Waespi, we have other maps of Gracac which would have worked better, but that explains further that marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. That's it, that's exactly what I meant to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Great. We would have a better one, P536. But if the witness is fine, an experienced policeman, with his markings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, did you follow -- if you say you took a bypass, was that a road which bypasses Gracac, down, a little bit under it, and then going up north again? Is that what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. We turned left here. There was a factory here, a huge silo, and then left up, whereas if we had taken a right turn we would have driven straight into Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If it could be marked, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't heard from any of the other Defence teams. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit P2696. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2696, a marked map, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vitez, there is evidence in this case that on the 7th of August, in Gracac, in the centre, the house of the UNMOs was set on fire. And there is also evidence that on the 6th of August, the residence of the UNMOs was on fire. And the residency of the of the UNMOs was about 1 kilometre east of the centre. Now, let's have a look at the photograph of the burning of the UNMO residence. And, Mr. President, this is P522. And you told us yesterday that, you know, you haven't seen any fresh damage, and perhaps you might have seen that by passing through or from a distance. Just tell us what you know.
